titleStmt.title: Trajectory of the main GABAergic interneuron populations from early development to old age in the rat primary auditory cortex
titleStmt.author: Ouellet
de Villers-Sidani

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Trajectory of the main GABAergic interneuron populations from early development to old age in the rat primary auditory cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how the populations expressing each interneuron marker change across the whole lifespan of the rat auditory cortex
span.quote: Only a handful of studies have however examined the impact of natural aging on the various cortical interneuron subtypes, most of them focusing on a small fraction of the interneuron pool (Miettinen et al., 1993 ; Bu et al., 2003 ; Pugliese et al., 2004 ; see Lehmann et al., 2012 for a review). As these changes strongly lend themselves to understanding the development of age-related inhibition-related disorders, it is thus critical to develop a full picture of how interneurons' populations naturally fluctuate.

span.label: which inhibitory subtypes decline with age, when, and in which cortical layers
span.quote: To best conceptualize these inherent lifecourse dynamics, we have documented the distribution of 7 different markers of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons on healthy Long-Evans rats from 9 days (P9) at five time point during the rats' life until advanced maturity at 25 months (P750, equivalent to ~75 human years based on this strain's longevity).

span.label: a lifespan trajectory for seven markers showing PV and SOM change most, with SOM peaking in young adulthood and falling back to juvenile levels by old age
span.quote: This analysis provided strong evidence that several but not all GABAergic neurons were affected by the aging process, showing most dramatic changes in expression of parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) expression.

span.label: existence
span.quote: This analysis provided strong evidence that several but not all GABAergic neurons were affected by the aging process, showing most dramatic changes in expression of parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) expression.

span.label: lifespan trajectories of GABAergic interneuron marker expression in primary auditory cortex
span.quote: Using the rat primary auditory cortex (A1) as a model, we probed the known markers of GABAergic interneurons with immunohistological methods, using antibodies against gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SOM), calretinin (CR), vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), neuropeptide Y (NPY), and cholecystokinin (CCK) to document the changes observed in interneuron populations across the rat's lifespan.

span.label: immunohistochemistry
span.quote: We determined the number of immune-labeled cells in each section of A1 at different ages (P9, P20, P120, P350, and P700–750) using the optical dissector method (StereoInvestigator software MBF bioscience, Williston, VT) to avoid biased sampling.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Programmed death of GABAergic interneurons drives the early cortical change in the excitation-inhibition balance
span.quote: In agreement with this possibility, we have found numerous lines of evidence to suggest that programmed GABAergic cell death in a variety of interneuron populations death may, in fact, provide an integral part of cortical changes (thus, by extension, excitability) across the life course.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Marker counts fall because cells down-regulate protein expression rather than because the cells die
span.quote: Rather than pure cell death, these results could also reflect a large down-regulation of protein expression, as evidenced by resurgence of PV in Kamal et al. ( 2013 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The auditory information content of the environment drives parvalbumin cells to up- or down-regulate their protein expression
span.quote: Both de Villers-Sidani et al. ( 2010 ) and Kamal et al. ( 2013 ) have shown that PV-containing cells are sensitive to environments carrying high and low auditory information, respectively, and can up- or down-regulate their characteristic protein expression accordingly.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: NPY-expressing cells up-regulate as a compensation for the loss of ChAT processes and the decay of PV and SOM expression
span.quote: NPY-expressing cells might thus have undertaken a compensatory mechanism for their ChAT counterparts, or more broadly for decay of PV and SOM expression.

span.label: marker counts can change without cell numbers changing, if subtypes up- or down-regulate the marker
span.quote: However, this finding also indicates that some interneuron subtypes may up- or down-regulate expression of certain markers, perhaps compensating for changes in cortical networks resulting from learning or degeneration.

span.label: the bulk of the PV expansion happens between P9 and P20, with two thirds of those cells in thalamorecipient layer 4
span.quote: The bulk of PV expression occurred as stated above between P9 and P20 with 2/3 of cells located in the thalamorecipient layer 4.

span.label: the mid-life SOM loss is specific to superficial layers 2/3, with no change elsewhere in that interval
span.quote: This change is primarily the result of a 50% disappearance of these cells in superficial layers 2/3. No significant change in SOM was noted in the other layers during that period.

span.label: late-life losses concentrate in output layers 5/6 for both PV and SOM
span.quote: Continuing to later life it was layers 5/6 that saw the greatest changes in both PV and SOM cells which were reduced by 32% ( p = 0.02; Figure 6 ) and 60% ( p = 006; Figure 6 ), respectively.

span.label: changes in PV, SOM and NPY are partly independent of total GABA, which is stable across the same late interval
span.quote: Total GABA+ and Nissl+ cell counts remained stable between P350 and P700, indicating against the changes in PV, SOM and NPY expression are to some extent independent from GABA staining fluctuations.

span.label: Only primary auditory cortex was examined, so the trajectories cannot be generalised to other brain regions.
span.quote: First, our observations were limited to A1, which, although mirroring structural and functional aspects of many other cortical areas cannot accurately speak to changes in other brain regions.

span.label: A single rat strain in a simple laboratory environment was used, and both factors are known to affect interneuron populations.
span.quote: Secondly, our study was conducted in single strain of rats living in a relatively simple laboratory environment.

span.label: Several interneuron markers were not examined.
span.quote: Additionally, our study did not systematically explore all possible interneuron markers, excluding, for example calbindin, NOS, doublecortin and 5-HT3.

span.label: GABA immunoreactivity may not reveal every inhibitory neuron, so the GABAergic totals are estimates.
span.quote: It should also be mentioned that GABA immunoreactivity may provide only an estimate of GABAergic population as some inhibitory neurons might in some circumstance not be revealed by such antibodies.

span.label: Low marker counts cannot be distinguished from low protein expression in existing cells.
span.quote: To reiterate, our study was not able to determine whether this reflects evidence of low cell populations per se , but may rather reflect differing protein elaboration.

span.label: the marker groups are not a partition: the percentages sum above 100 and the same neuron may be counted under several markers
span.quote: It is important to note that all neurons taken together, these percentages add up to more than 100%, confirming that individual neurons express multiple markers and that the same neurons may have been were counted more than once for different markers

span.label: the seven markers cover about 90% of interneurons, so a tenth of the population is unaccounted for
span.quote: Together these markers reveal around 90% of the overall cortical interneuron population (Gonchar et al., 2008 ; Xu et al., 2010 ; Rudy et al., 2011 ). PV, SOM and CR are useful to divide the interneurons in three mostly non-overlapping groups, which can then be further characterized with the additional markers

span.label: A1 was functionally mapped only in a subset of animals, and at P9 the location was borrowed from P12 because tones evoke no response yet
span.quote: Functional mapping was performed in at least one animal at every age examined except for P9 where tone-evoked responses cannot yet be obtained. For that group, the location of A1 was determined based on mapping done at P12.

span.label: some declines in total GABA cannot be explained by the marker populations that changed, which are too few in absolute number
span.quote: The total number of GABA+ cells also decreased by ~20% (12.1 ± 0.3 to 9.6 ± 0.2 cells/hpf; p = 0.02; Figure 1 ) during the same period, a change that cannot be fully explained the trajectories of SOM or NPY cells which are to few in absolute numbers to influence global GABA counts to this extent.

span.label: an estimated twenty interneuron subtypes exist, so seven markers describe a coarse partition of a finer reality
span.quote: It is estimated that as many of 20 subtypes exist, representing a broad range of morphology and function

span.label: the lifespan trajectory as a unit of analysis, rather than a comparison between two ages
span.quote: To best conceptualize these inherent lifecourse dynamics, we have documented the distribution of 7 different markers of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons on healthy Long-Evans rats from 9 days (P9) at five time point during the rats' life until advanced maturity at 25 months (P750, equivalent to ~75 human years based on this strain's longevity).

span.label: turning the measured trajectories into a simple model of inhibitory signalling over life
span.quote: With this evidence, we show how understanding these trajectories of cell counts may be factored into a simple model to quantify changes in inhibitory signaling across the course of life, which may be applied as a framework for creating more advanced simulations of interneuronal implication in normal cerebral processing, normal aging, or pathological processes.

span.label: ChAT → VIP
span.note: PARTIAL, AND MEASURED AT ABOUT HALF: in A1, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ cells were also VIP+ - against previous visual-cortex work reporting that ChAT co-localises INVARIABLY with VIP. The overlap is a fact about a marker pair in one area, and the paper reports it as a difference from the visual cortex. The reliability layer distinguishes full from partial overlap; the concept layer's equivalence types do not.
span.quote: In previous studies focusing on the visual cortex, ChAT has been found to invariably co-localize to cells expressing VIP (Gonchar et al., 2008 ). We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+

span.label: a PV cell here is a cell staining for parvalbumin at one moment - the paper is explicit that this counts MARKER EXPRESSION and that expression may be regulated up or down independently of cell number
span.quote: However, this finding also indicates that some interneuron subtypes may up- or down-regulate expression of certain markers, perhaps compensating for changes in cortical networks resulting from learning or degeneration.

span.label: the marker categories OVERLAP - percentages across markers sum to more than 100% and individual cells are counted more than once, so PV, SOM, VIP and the rest are not disjoint classes
span.quote: It is important to note that all neurons taken together, these percentages add up to more than 100%, confirming that individual neurons express multiple markers and that the same neurons may have been were counted more than once for different markers

span.label: ChAT and VIP colocalise invariably in visual cortex and only about half the time here, so a marker relationship established in one area does not carry to another
span.quote: In previous studies focusing on the visual cortex, ChAT has been found to invariably co-localize to cells expressing VIP (Gonchar et al., 2008 ). We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+

span.label: GABA positivity is treated as definitional for these markers, with one developmental exception: a quarter of CR cells at P9 are GABA-negative
span.quote: We also found that a subset CR+ cells at P9 were GABA− (24 ± 6%) whereas all of them were GABA+ at later ages.

span.label: all percentages are shares of a shrinking denominator - total GABA cells fall sharply before P20 - so proportional stability and absolute stability come apart
span.quote: Thus, GABA positive cells saw their overall representation in the neuronal pool fall from 16 to 12% over that time period.

span.label: method: immunohistochemistry for seven interneuron markers plus GABA and Nissl, counted in 21 random fields per animal across functionally identified A1
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: immunohistochemistry — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: For the cell count analysis, 21 photomicrographs were taken in each animal at random locations within the borders of A1 with on average equal sampling in all cortical layers.

span.label: phenomenon: age-related change in cortical inhibitory populations
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: lifespan trajectories of GABAergic interneuron marker expression in primary auditory cortex — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: However, the study and quantification of interneuron dynamics in neuropathology is complicated by natural fluctuations in their population over the lifecourse

span.label: replicates → Pinto et al. (2010) (stability of the basal human GABA pool across the lifespan)
span.quote: These results mirror with studies by Pinto et al. ( 2010 ) that confirmed that the basal pool of GABA in human is relatively maintained across the lifespan.

span.label: replicates → Gonchar et al., 2008 (layer-based changes in CR, VIP and ChAT cells in mouse)
span.quote: Also in agreement with earlier studies in mouse (Gonchar et al., 2008 ), there were layer-based changes in cells expressing other neuropeptides (CR, VIP, ChAT).

span.label: contradicts → Cha et al., 1996, 1997 (human findings on NPY with age)
span.quote: Surprisingly and unexpectedly given previous findings from humans (Cha et al., 1996 , 1997 ), NPY showed a significant increase between P20 and P350.

span.label: contradicts → Gonchar et al., 2008 (invariable ChAT/VIP co-localisation in visual cortex)
span.quote: In previous studies focusing on the visual cortex, ChAT has been found to invariably co-localize to cells expressing VIP (Gonchar et al., 2008 ). We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+ (48 ± 6%; Figure 2 ).

span.label: extends → studies documenting interneuron distributions at single time points, by following seven markers across a full lifespan
span.quote: Only a handful of studies have however examined the impact of natural aging on the various cortical interneuron subtypes, most of them focusing on a small fraction of the interneuron pool (Miettinen et al., 1993 ; Bu et al., 2003 ; Pugliese et al., 2004 ; see Lehmann et al., 2012 for a review). As these changes strongly lend themselves to understanding the development of age-related inhibition-related disorders, it is thus critical to develop a full picture of how interneurons' populations naturally fluctuate.

span.label: contradicts → the visual-cortex finding that ChAT invariably colocalises with VIP
span.quote: In previous studies focusing on the visual cortex, ChAT has been found to invariably co-localize to cells expressing VIP (Gonchar et al., 2008 ). We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+

span.label: confirms → human work reporting that the basal GABA pool is broadly maintained across the lifespan
span.quote: However, this finding also indicates that some interneuron subtypes may up- or down-regulate expression of certain markers, perhaps compensating for changes in cortical networks resulting from learning or degeneration.

span.label: supports → accounts in which interneuron dysfunction underlies schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy and autism
span.quote: The study of how these interneurons contribute to ongoing cortical processing is still in its infancy, yet it is believed that their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases (Sanacora et al., 2000 ; McBain and Fisahn, 2001 ; Levitt et al., 2004 ; Marin, 2012 ) such as schizophrenia (Lewis, 2000 ; Lewis et al., 2005 ), Alzheimer's disease (Verret et al., 2012 ; Hazra et al., 2013 ), epilepsy (Cossart et al., 2001 ; Levitt, 2005 ) or autism spectrum disorder

span.label: builds-on → layer-based interneuron findings in mouse
span.quote: For both of these cell types the main change between P20 and P120 was a significant increase in their populations in output layers 5/6 (PV: 50% increase; p = 0.01; SOM: 290% increase; p < 0.001; Figure 6 ).

span.label: PV —part-of→ GABA
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — every marked cell was GABA-positive, with the P9 calretinin exception noted separately
span.quote: GABA co-labeling was also examined for all interneuron markers at all ages and except for one exception (see CR results below), all cells positive for one of the markers examined were also GABA immunoreactive

span.label: CR —part-of→ GABA
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — SCOPED: a quarter of CR cells at P9 are GABA-negative, and all are positive later. The containment is developmental, not definitional
span.quote: We also found that a subset CR+ cells at P9 were GABA− (24 ± 6%) whereas all of them were GABA+ at later ages.

span.label: PV —distinct-from→ SOM
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — CRITERION UNDERMINED: marker percentages sum above 100% and cells are counted more than once, so these groups are not disjoint
span.quote: It is important to note that all neurons taken together, these percentages add up to more than 100%, confirming that individual neurons express multiple markers and that the same neurons may have been were counted more than once for different markers

span.label: RETRACTED (A MEASURED PARTIAL OVERLAP, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS THE PAPER'S POINT) · ChAT —same-as→ VIP
span.note: RETRACTED: A MEASURED PARTIAL OVERLAP, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS THE PAPER'S POINT. The edge is `ChAT --same-as--> VIP`. The span reports that previous visual-cortex work found ChAT 'to INVARIABLY co-localize to cells expressing VIP', and then: 'We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, ONLY ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+.' The word `only` is the author marking the departure. HALF IS NOT SAMENESS, and a `same-as` edge records the claim this paper is correcting rather than the one it makes. WHAT THE SPAN DOES SAY (Q-309): housed below, with the number. — strength of the relation: 0.5 — the record marks this weak — CRITERION: invariable colocalisation in visual cortex, about 50% here. An identity that holds in one area and not another
span.quote: In previous studies focusing on the visual cortex, ChAT has been found to invariably co-localize to cells expressing VIP (Gonchar et al., 2008 ). We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+

span.label: cells/hpf —operationalised-as→ PV
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — the count measures MARKER EXPRESSION; the paper says explicitly that subtypes may regulate the marker independently of their number
span.quote: However, this finding also indicates that some interneuron subtypes may up- or down-regulate expression of certain markers, perhaps compensating for changes in cortical networks resulting from learning or degeneration.

span.label: aging —causes→ SOM
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — SIGN: falling after P120, back to juvenile levels by old age
span.quote: During that period we observed a substantial ~50% decrease in SOM expression (down to 1.5 ± 0.3 cells/hpf; p = 0.04; Figure 4 ) and a continued increase of NPY+ cells

span.label: aging —causes→ NPY
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — SIGN: rising, opposite in direction to SOM over the same interval
span.quote: NPY expression also steadily increased from P20 to P120 by more than three-fold (0.19 ± 0.04 to 0.74 ± 0.3 cells/hpf; p = 0.03; Figure 3 ).

span.label: aging —causes→ PV
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — SIGN: falling, but only late and by 23%
span.quote: During that later life period PV+ cell counts also declined significantly by 23%

span.label: PV —part-of→ layer 4
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — two thirds of the early PV expansion lands in the thalamorecipient layer
span.quote: The bulk of PV expression occurred as stated above between P9 and P20 with 2/3 of cells located in the thalamorecipient layer 4.

span.label: PV —causes→ critical period
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — a role imported from the plasticity literature, not tested here
span.quote: PV-positive cells have been implicated in initiation of a critical period for cortical plasticity in the visual, somatosensory and auditory cortices (Hensch et al., 1998 ; Fagiolini and Hensch, 2000 ; Hensch, 2004 , 2005 ; Fox and Wong, 2005 ; Yuste, 2005 ; Wonders and Anderson, 2006 ; de Villers-Sidani et al., 2008 ; Lehmann et al., 2012 ) and play a critical role in cortical information processing (Tallon-Baudry et al., 1998 ; Bartos et al., 2007 ; Cardin et al., 2009 ; Sohal et al., 2009 ), whereas SOM-positive cells are believed to plays a role in the acquisition memory and emotional functions

span.label: Nissl —contrasted-with→ GABA
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — both stable in late life, which is what makes the marker changes over the same period independent of overall cell loss
span.quote: Total GABA+ and Nissl+ cell counts remained stable between P350 and P700, indicating against the changes in PV, SOM and NPY expression are to some extent independent from GABA staining fluctuations.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Statistical significance between the different age groups and for curve fitting was assessed using ANOVA analysis and the F -test.

span.label: regression (least squares)
span.quote: Regression analysis was performed in the MatLab environment (Natick, MA) and using the least square methods.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Unless stated otherwise, data are presented as mean ± standard error to the mean (s.e.m).

span.label: coefficient of determination
span.quote: R 2 regression values are shown in each graph for the exponential function fit (left) and linear function fit (right).

span.label: root mean square error
span.quote: RMSE stands for root mean square error.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: Time constant of exponential decay (t½; days ± 95% confidence intervals)

span.label: unbiased stereological sampling
span.quote: We determined the number of immune-labeled cells in each section of A1 at different ages (P9, P20, P120, P350, and P700–750) using the optical dissector method (StereoInvestigator software MBF bioscience, Williston, VT) to avoid biased sampling.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: During that later life period PV+ cell counts also declined significantly by 23% ( p = 0.02; Figure 4 ).

span.label: s.e.m.
span.quote: For the cell count analysis, 21 photomicrographs were taken in each animal at random locations within the borders of A1 with on average equal sampling in all cortical layers.

span.label: p < 0.001
span.quote: Surprisingly, we found that even though there was considerable variance between different populations at different time points, the total number of cortical neuron and inhibitory neurons as evidenced by neuron specific Nissl and GABA staining decrease rapidly before postnatal day 20 (P20), by 41 and 77% respectively but afterward remained unchanged (Nissl: from 155 ± 5 to 110 ± 4 cells/hpf; p < 0.001; GABA: from 24 ± 3 to 13 ± 2 cells/hpf; p < 0.001; Figure 1 ).

span.label: Both total Nissl-stained neuron counts and total GABA+ counts in A1 dropped sharply before P20 (155 to 110 and 24 to 13 cells per high-power field) and then stayed flat for the rest of life.
span.quote: Surprisingly, we found that even though there was considerable variance between different populations at different time points, the total number of cortical neuron and inhibitory neurons as evidenced by neuron specific Nissl and GABA staining decrease rapidly before postnatal day 20 (P20), by 41 and 77% respectively but afterward remained unchanged (Nissl: from 155 ± 5 to 110 ± 4 cells/hpf; p < 0.001; GABA: from 24 ± 3 to 13 ± 2 cells/hpf; p < 0.001; Figure 1 ).

span.label: Aging affected only some interneuron classes, with parvalbumin and somatostatin expression showing by far the largest changes.
span.quote: This analysis provided strong evidence that several but not all GABAergic neurons were affected by the aging process, showing most dramatic changes in expression of parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) expression.

span.label: The parvalbumin-positive population expanded 450% between P9 and P20.
span.quote: Another notable change between P9 and P20 was the significant 450% expansion of the PV cell population ( p < 0.001; Figure 4 ).

span.label: By P20 parvalbumin cells were the dominant interneuron type in A1 at roughly 35% of the population, ahead of VIP (18%) and calretinin (10%).
span.quote: At P20, as seen in Figures 5 , 6 , PV+ cells became by far the dominant interneuron in A1 representing around 35% of the overall population followed by the CR (10%) and VIP (18%) populations.

span.label: Somatostatin cell counts kept rising after P20 and peaked at about P120 at 2.75 cells per high-power field, roughly double their P20 value.
span.quote: SOM+ cell counts however continued to increase and reached their lifetime maximum at around P120 (~100% increase to 2.75 ± 0.2; p = 0.01; Figure 4 ).

span.label: Between P120 and P350 somatostatin expression fell by about half while NPY cells continued to increase.
span.quote: During that period we observed a substantial ~50% decrease in SOM expression (down to 1.5 ± 0.3 cells/hpf; p = 0.04; Figure 4 ) and a continued increase of NPY+ cells (up to 1.1 ± 0.3 cells/hpf; p = 0.04; Figure 3 ).

span.label: The mid-life fall in somatostatin cells came almost entirely from a 50% loss in superficial layers 2/3.
span.quote: This change is primarily the result of a 50% disappearance of these cells in superficial layers 2/3.

span.label: Parvalbumin cell counts declined significantly by 23% in the oldest animals.
span.quote: During that later life period PV+ cell counts also declined significantly by 23% ( p = 0.02; Figure 4 ).

span.label: In late life the largest losses of both parvalbumin and somatostatin cells occurred in output layers 5/6, which fell by 32% and 60% respectively.
span.quote: Continuing to later life it was layers 5/6 that saw the greatest changes in both PV and SOM cells which were reduced by 32% ( p = 0.02; Figure 6 ) and 60% ( p = 006; Figure 6 ), respectively.

span.label: NPY was the only marker whose expression kept increasing from birth into old age.
span.quote: Confirming our earlier results, the linear function fitted to NPY measurements is consistent with a progressive increase in their expression throughout the lifespan.

span.label: Marker trajectories fell into four shapes: inverse exponential decay then plateau (CCK), inverse exponential decay then linear increase (NPY), exponential decay then plateau (ChAT, VIP, CR), and inverse exponential decay then linear decrease (PV, SOM).
span.quote: At the most simple level, changes in interneuron marker expression may be grouped into four distinct categories: inverse exponential decay and plateau (CCK), inverse exponential decay and linear increase (NPY), exponential decay and plateau (ChAT, VIP, and CR), and inverse exponential decay followed by linear decrease (PV and SOM).

span.label: An exponential decay function described marker counts over the first 150 days of life, whereas a linear function fitted the P150-750 period better.
span.quote: Based on goodness of fit measures (Table 2 ), we first determined that the variation in interneuron markers could be reasonably well described by an exponential decay function in the first 150 days of life whereas a linear function was a better fit for P150–750.

span.label: Contrary to reports in visual cortex, only about half of ChAT-positive cells in A1 also expressed VIP, at every age tested.
span.quote: We examined here if it was also the case in A1 and found that, at all ages, only ~50% of ChAT+ were also VIP+ (48 ± 6%; Figure 2 ).

span.label: At P9 about a quarter of calretinin-positive cells were GABA-negative, whereas at all later ages every calretinin cell was GABA-positive.
span.quote: We also found that a subset CR+ cells at P9 were GABA− (24 ± 6%) whereas all of them were GABA+ at later ages.

span.label: Total cortical GABAergic cell numbers were essentially unchanged after P350 even though the two largest subtypes, PV and SOM, were disappearing.
span.quote: Our finding can support this interpretation that, despite widespread disappearance of the two most prominent GABAergic interneuron types, PV and SOM, numbers of cortical GABAergic cells remained essentially unchanged after P350.

span.label: total neuron and GABA counts fall sharply before P20 and are broadly stable afterwards
span.quote: Surprisingly, we found that even though there was considerable variance between different populations at different time points, the total number of cortical neuron and inhibitory neurons as evidenced by neuron specific Nissl and GABA staining decrease rapidly before postnatal day 20 (P20), by 41 and 77% respectively but afterward remained unchanged (Nissl: from 155 ± 5 to 110 ± 4 cells/hpf; p < 0.001; GABA: from 24 ± 3 to 13 ± 2 cells/hpf; p < 0.001; Figure 1 ).

span.label: GABA cells fall from about 16% to about 12% of the neuron pool over that early period
span.quote: Thus, GABA positive cells saw their overall representation in the neuronal pool fall from 16 to 12% over that time period.

span.label: PV expanded 450% between P9 and P20 and became the dominant marked population at about 35%
span.quote: Another notable change between P9 and P20 was the significant 450% expansion of the PV cell population ( p < 0.001; Figure 4 ). At P20, as seen in Figures 5 , 6 , PV+ cells became by far the dominant interneuron in A1 representing around 35% of the overall population followed by the CR (10%) and VIP (18%) populations.

span.label: SOM peaked at P120 at roughly double its P20 level
span.quote: SOM+ cell counts however continued to increase and reached their lifetime maximum at around P120 (~100% increase to 2.75 ± 0.2; p = 0.01; Figure 4 ).

span.label: SOM fell about 50% between P120 and P350 and by old age was back to its P20 value
span.quote: As the animals grew into old age, the same trends continued including a further reduction in SOM+ cells (down to 0.9 ± 0.3 cells/hpf; p = 0.009; Figure 4 ), now not significantly different from their P20 value

span.label: NPY rose more than threefold from P20 to P120 and kept rising into old age
span.quote: NPY expression also steadily increased from P20 to P120 by more than three-fold (0.19 ± 0.04 to 0.74 ± 0.3 cells/hpf; p = 0.03; Figure 3 ).

span.label: PV declined 23% only in later life
span.quote: During that later life period PV+ cell counts also declined significantly by 23%

span.label: at P9 the dominant markers were CR, VIP and ChAT, with PV, SOM, NPY and CCK barely expressed
span.quote: At P9, CR, VIP, and ChAT appeared to be the most prominent cortical interneuron markers; representing 10, 8, and 1% of total GABA positive cells (see Figure 2 ). This finding may be explained by delayed postnatal development of the most common markers in adults, PV, SOM, NPY and CCK, which were still minimally expressed in that second week of age.

span.label: the mid-life SOM loss came almost entirely from superficial layers 2/3
span.quote: This change is primarily the result of a 50% disappearance of these cells in superficial layers 2/3. No significant change in SOM was noted in the other layers during that period.

span.label: late-life losses in both PV and SOM concentrated in output layers 5/6
span.quote: Continuing to later life it was layers 5/6 that saw the greatest changes in both PV and SOM cells which were reduced by 32% ( p = 0.02; Figure 6 ) and 60% ( p = 006; Figure 6 ), respectively.
